p.t: In short
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t:
Treat every idea as a guess. **Test it** before you trust it.
Set a **fixed test budget** before you start. Only spend money you can afford to lose.
Set your **stop rules** (rules for when to drop a product) before you spend. Then follow them.

Test **one product at a time**. Expect several failed products before one winner (a product that sells at a profit).
Most early tests lose money before one wins. Plan for that.

Set a stop rule (kill rule) before you test, then follow it.
Judge products by the numbers, not by how much you like them.

Keep testing many products. One win or one loss does not decide the business.
Wait about three weeks before making big changes.
Testing culture and hypotheses
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t: No ad strategy is a silver bullet (a magic fix that always works).
Mentors give educated guesses (informed guesses based on experience), so **every opinion must be tested**.
Treat each recommendation as a hypothesis (a proposed explanation that still needs proof), not as a fact.

Testing produces proof for decisions. Advice from tools and mentors only gives guidelines.
When you are unsure and the budget allows, **test**.
When the budget is limited, put money where it already converts (turns visitors into buyers).

Treat every idea as a hypothesis, and **test it rather than debate it**.
Rejecting an untested idea should require a detailed written argument.

The default is to run the test.
Treat every ad test as a hypothesis.
Decide on the one **variable** (the single thing you change) to test.

Keep the other things the same.
Early numbers are an educated guess until more data arrives.
A hypothesis is a proposed explanation based on limited evidence (little information) that must be tested.
Form it by reading the data, looking at the creative (the ad image or video), and thinking about where the ad falls short.

Then test that single hypothesis against a **control** (an unchanged version to compare with).
Large companies **test everything**. They do not reject ideas without evidence.

Some results surprise you, even though they look obvious afterwards.
So **test against your hypothesis** rather than dismissing it.
Research and testing are the two pillars (main supports) of finding a winning ad.

Research shows who the audience (the people an ad is shown to) is and what language they use.
Testing shows what actually sells.
Research before building. Look at the brand's ads, page and offers.
Then estimate its numbers with a simple spreadsheet and **conservative inputs** (cautious, low guesses).
Testing culture and hypotheses (continued)
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t:
This gives a clear view of the opportunity before you spend money.
No single product research method is perfect.

**Use the method that has worked in your own tests**. Do not copy someone else's routine exactly.
Testing is the basics, not quick tricks.
No single method is perfect. The goal is to **raise your odds** with more proof of concept (proof that an idea can work).

Judge each product by the evidence collected, not by intuition (gut feeling).
Constant testing is the approach.
Test angles (the main message of an ad), ad videos and products again and again. Keep what converts.
Organic (free, unpaid) growth depends more on **repeated testing** than on one perfect video.

Find and test products systematically, rather than repeating a few products.
Repeated testing of a few products without a method wastes time and money.

Facebook ads are not a fixed science with guaranteed rules.
Verify results with **ongoing tests**.

Market conditions change, so continuous testing is a standard part of the process.
Intuition and personal taste often misjudge what the market will buy.

Check ideas by **response**, not by how good they seem.
Expect to be wrong often. Let results correct the plan.
A product can look weak and still sell.

Trust the data over your own opinion.
**Test the product yourself with ads** before rejecting it.

Use **data, not emotion**, for every decision in the ad account and on the store.
This includes changes to ads, pages and budgets.

Treat the numbers on the screen as the only signal of whether something works.
Base decisions on factual data rather than gut feeling.
Keep learning from mistakes.
The mentor said analytical habits (habits of checking numbers) are a major advantage for founders starting in e-commerce (selling online).

Only trust an ad when its tracked cost per customer is known.
Assuming a long-running ad is the best ad, without checking its results, **wastes money**.

Some campaigns run on habit, not data.
Test creatives, the landing page (the page a click opens) and the offer **separately**.
Testing culture and hypotheses (continued)
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t:
Change **one asset at a time**, judged on its own metric (the number that measures it).
Do not guess.
**Diagnose before changing anything.**

**Change one variable at a time.**
If several things change together, you cannot know which change caused the result.
Before spending real money, test a new store setup or ad idea with a dummy store (a fake test copy) or dummy ad.

Move to a live store with a real paid ad **only after each step is understood**.
Record every test in a notebook or document so results can be compared later.

Compare each new product test with data from earlier tests.
Build a **repeatable routine**: test, read the metrics (the key numbers), and improve.

Over time, this routine builds the skills to recognise winners faster.
Small, well-chosen changes can add up to large results.
Examples are title keywords (search words in the product title), dynamic retargeting (showing ads again to people who already visited, with the products they viewed), and opt-ins (email sign-ups).

**Focus on these levers** before chasing new tactics.
Competitor optimisation happens gradually.

Repeat the competitor review (checking rival stores) about **every two weeks**.
Make small improvements to the store over time, instead of fixing everything at once.

Constant testing trains video skills such as hooks (the first seconds that stop people scrolling) and angles.
These skills transfer to the next product.

Early tests are practice. This makes it faster to **scale** (spend more on) a winning product later.
Expect to test many ideas. Not every idea will work.

Keep testing, measure the results, and **adjust quickly**.
Do not wait for a perfect plan.
**Test one product at a time**, and read the result honestly.

A failed test is feedback, not failure.
Test, refine (improve details), and improve until the product or approach wins.
Two approaches exist.

Option A: invest deeply in one product that can become a brand.
Option B: test many products quickly to find a winner, then build a brand around it.
Winning in dropshipping (selling products that a supplier ships to customers, so you hold no stock) comes from **volume and speed of testing**.

Not from perfect products or perfect ads.
A stalled result shows what does not work, and brings you closer to what does.
Testing budget and capital
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t: Set a **firm testing budget** before you buy traffic (paid visitors) for product tests.
Avoid spending large amounts on tests that do not follow the research method.

In the mentor's example, unfocused tests on other markets and platforms cost about **$500** in total.
Disciplined testing lost only about $100.

Testing requires spending money, because product results only show up after real spend.
Set a **fixed test budget in advance**.

Judge the product on that data, not on the first few clicks.
Only test with budget you **can afford to lose**.
Small samples (small amounts of data) give noisy results.

The testing period also needs enough spend before the data can be trusted.
Set a fixed testing budget that you can afford to lose completely.

Decide in advance that losing it will not upset you.
Do not treat the budget as a limit that ends the business once it is spent.
Before seeing any profit, a beginner should expect to lose **about $2,000** in testing, or whatever amount their budget is.

The lower the starting budget, the smaller the expected loss.
Write this expectation down before starting.
Losses grow with business size.

A larger operation may lose $30,000 or $200,000 in testing.
Losing money is a normal cost of doing business, not a sign to quit.

Giving yourself a budget and quitting once it is spent is the **wrong approach**.
Accept the testing budget as expendable (money you can use up).

Keep testing.
When testing a new product, spend **no more than 50 percent** of your available investment capital (money set aside to invest) on the test.
For example, with 5,000 USD in capital, keep at least half in reserve (money kept aside).
How long to test before judging depends on your personal budget and how much risk you can take.

Products can fail quickly, so keep spare capital rather than going all in.
Test a new product on a **small budget first**, to see whether the market responds.
Testing an untested product with the full budget means risking it all on an unknown outcome.
Testing budget and capital (continued)
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t:
Test **one product per week** with a budget of about 200 to 300 USD per product.
Keep going until there is enough data to either move on or keep trying.

Ad spend on a product with zero sales is **learning money, not lost money**.
Move on after about **300 USD** of spend with zero sales.
Spending profits as soon as they arrive, or switching between many new ventures, starves the core business.
Keep the budget for the next product, and for branding the current store.

Plan a fixed test budget and a schedule in advance for influencer campaigns (paid posts by people with followers).
Do not spend freely.

Influencer campaigns often fail. Some of the first creators contacted will not convert (will not bring sales).
Keep the first sales **only as proof**.

The core is a repeatable process: test products, read results, move on.
Spending on research tools and paid training is a trap.

The main work is **testing ads with real budgets**.
Research can show ideas, but only ads prove them.
Early paid testing minimum: about 100 clicks per product is too small a sample for a firm conclusion.
Treat the first 100 clicks as a learning and optimisation (tuning) period.

Test early ads over an extended period (about **25 days at 10 dollars per day** for a product) before dropping it.
Include optimisation time.

Do not stop at a fixed dollar amount if sales are missing.
Test before scaling: start with a small test budget, and only scale an approach if it performs.
Each ad account is different, so **CBO** (one budget for the whole campaign) may not work.
**ABO** (a separate budget for each ad set, meaning each group of ads with one audience and budget) or other scaling methods may be needed.

Getting comfortable with large ad budgets is part of scaling a profitable store.
Spend levels that seem extreme at the start can be necessary to grow tenfold later.
Kill rules and stop criteria
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t:
Set **kill rules** (rules that say when to drop a product) before you test it, and follow them.
Keeping a product you like, without results, wastes time.

A product with a strong visual wow factor but no clear problem it solves often gets views without sales.
Set **cut rules** before the test starts, and follow them strictly.

A failing product blocks budget that another product could use.
A strong product can make **5-10 sales** on day one.

Stop a product that keeps losing money after a set test budget.
Do not hope for a turnaround.

Fixed stop rules keep the test budget away from unproven products.
Set a clear kill rule **before spending** on a new product.

If a product gets no sales after a fixed test spend and a few days of ads, **cut it**.
Move to the next product instead of pouring more money in.

Kill a product early when it shows no signs.
Test about **$50 to $100** on day one, with a maximum of $200 to $250.
On TikTok, consider killing it around $60 if creatives and CTR (click-through rate, the share of viewers who click) are poor.
Give a product **3 to 5 days** after fixing the offer (the deal you sell) and the store.
If about **$200** has been spent across 10 to 15 audiences at $5 to $10 per day (an audience is the group of people an ad shows to) without any sign of profitability, move on to the next product.
Spend is one of the limits, but **the numbers decide**.
Before running ads, know three numbers: COGS (cost of goods sold, what the product costs you), break-even return on ad spend (the sales per dollar you need so you do not lose money),

and break-even cost per purchase (the most you can spend on ads per sale).
These numbers set the limits for every later scaling decision.
**Switch off an ad** that spends past its margin (profit left per sale after costs) without a sale.
In the example below, the margin is too thin to scale at the current CPA (cost per acquisition, the ad cost of one sale).
So also raise average order value (the average money per order).

**Kill thresholds from different stages (sources do not conflict; each applies at a different stage):**
**Day one, no signs**

Threshold: $50 to $100; maximum $200 to $250
When it applies: Facebook test, no signs on day one
**TikTok, poor creatives and CTR**

Threshold: About $60
When it applies: TikTok test with weak creatives and CTR
**Offer and store fixed**
Kill rules and stop criteria (continued)
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t:
Threshold: About $200 across 10 to 15 audiences at $5 to $10 per day, after 3 to 5 days
When it applies: No sign of profitability
**Zero sales after spend**

Threshold: About $300
When it applies: Product with no sales; treat spend as learning money
**Per-product test budget**

Threshold: About $200 to $250 to $300
When it applies: One product per week until there is enough data
**Share of capital**

Threshold: Maximum 50 percent of investment capital
When it applies: Per new product test

Do not drop a product too early when its ads show some views (people seeing them).
The breakthrough can come unexpectedly after a stretch of low results.

In the example case, the seller was close to quitting just before the product **exploded** (suddenly took off).
Judge a product by its early signals.
If it gets views but no sales after the normal test window, **extend the test by one more week**.

If it gets neither views nor engagement (likes, comments, clicks), and you doubt it converts, **drop it** and move to the next product.
Do not close ad sets too early.

Some ad sets only convert after spend passes a certain amount, for example after the 12th dollar.
Give ad sets patience while CTR is good.
Be patient with higher-ticket products (more expensive items), for example a $59.99 price.
The pixel (tracking code on the store that reports sales to the ad platform) needs time to collect data.
Give the ads more spend before closing them, **as long as CTR is above 1.5%**.
The 2% CTR case: one seller started with a product costing $26.99 that sold for $49.99. That leaves a **$23 margin**.

On the first day of Facebook ads, they got a **2% CTR** and no sales.
On day two, they ran six ad sets with $10 each, with a $20 offer running.

Advice given: **switch off an ad** that spends past its margin without a sale.
Also raise average order value with a bundle (several products sold together as one package).

A margin of about $23 makes scaling hard when CPA is $15 to $20.
Quality of testing matters more than volume in the early phase.

A product tested with only a few attempts gives little information.
Set a clear test-count target before deciding a product is not a winner, for example **20 to 30 products** rather than three.

Judging a new product after only **one week and one sale** is too early.
This is especially true if several offers have not been tested yet.

Early signals and dropping: a product with weak early signals should not be kept out of hope.
Early signals decide the next step.
Early signals and when to judge
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t:
Procedure for a new product that performs weakly:
1. Run a new product for the first couple of days.
2. **Check** its performance against your KPIs (key performance indicators, the key numbers you track).

3. If performance is weak, send your data to coaches or mentors for evaluation.
4. Wait for their assessment and feedback.

5. Follow their recommendation to either cut the product or continue testing.
In one case, poor early results were kept too long.
The team saw weak performance within two to three days.
They changed the background and angle on day three. That is early enough to **pivot** (change direction).

Daily results swing between green and red days (good and bad days).
Do **not cut a campaign after one red day**.

Add more creatives, and let the system keep learning.
A slow week after sales in past weeks can be normal.
Check the **funnel** (the path from click to sale): queries (search terms that show interest), add-to-cart (people who put an item in the cart), and checkout intent (people who start checkout).

Follow the troubleshooting steps (fix steps) before making changes.
Low ad spend produces slower data.

A small budget will not quickly show whether a product works.
Judge test results **only after enough spend has produced enough data**.

Early traffic behaviour is random at low volume.
A new store may make two or three sales in the first days, then go weeks without a sale.

Let data build up for about **three weeks** before major changes.
A low number of sales can come from a sample too small to read.

The first step is to **grow traffic** before judging a store as failed.
When few sales come in, do not change niches (narrow markets) right away.

First add more approved suppliers.
Then optimise ads (improve them) on the products that already get quality clicks.
The first sales depend on traffic, not on a fixed amount of time.
Once a store receives around **100 unique visitors** (different people) from Google Shopping (Google's product ads), the conversion target can be checked.
Early signals and when to judge (continued)
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t:
Note: this advice is from 2020 and is older.
Winning products are found through **fast, repeated product testing**.
A beginner may need several failed products (for example around eight) before finding a winner.
Judge a hook only after **repeated uploads** of the same format with variations (small changes), usually three to six times.

Ad videos that look weak early can still produce a breakout (sudden big growth).
One successful video can lift the whole account's follower count.

Influencer results are not always visible right away.
Be patient while the sales funnel works.
Use the full funnel to qualify influencers (check whether they fit) over a longer period, rather than judging a single post.

A product that works at first, then stops being profitable when scaled, is normal.
**Drop it**, launch the next product, and record what you learned from each product.

Then the next launch is better.
A single viral result (sudden huge spread) does not prove a product will last.

Keep testing new products and angles to build a consistent pipeline (a steady flow of tests).
Winning on TikTok is not a single lucky product.

In the example group, nobody found one product and executed it properly on the first try.
The chance of a hit rises with the number of products tested.

Dropshipping results come from testing, not from research alone.
Do not give up on a product too early, but keep checking the data.

Ad spend on a product with zero sales is learning money, as noted above.
Use the first sales only as proof of the process, not as the goal.
A case with strong early revenue (money coming in): one operator reached roughly **$1,000 in daily revenue** on the second day after launching a new product.
That result came only after testing more than twelve products before finding the first winner.
Pinterest case: a dropshipping product in another account generated **over $2,000** in its first week on Pinterest.
Its ROAS (return on ad spend, the sales earned per dollar spent) was about 4.5 shortly after launch.
Testing was done with a small daily budget, and the account was still in the **learning stage** (the ad platform was still learning who to show ads to).
One product at a time
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t:
Beginners should **test one product at a time**, with one account per product.
Running several products in parallel splits attention.

It makes the learning curve harder to manage.
Test one product at a time with **full focus**.
Move to a new product only after the current one fails to get traction (gain attention and sales) within about **one to two weeks**.
Once a product converts, keep it, and open more accounts to push it rather than switching products.

When working alone, test one product at a time for about two weeks, with **two products at most**.
Spreading small effort across many products usually fails.

Commit fully to one product, then expand once you are more experienced.
Testing one product at a time is the discipline.
Testing a single product, deciding it is a scam or saturated (the market is full and buyers are tired of it), and quitting is the most common failure pattern.
Testing multiple different products in rapid succession, instead of focusing on one product through all six phases (stages of the method), disrupts the learning cycle.

It prevents reaching profitability by Phase 6.
Consistency requires staying with one product long enough to gather meaningful data.

Testing sequence for one winning candidate (a product that looks promising):
1. Test one product at a time.
2. Try different store designs.

3. Try different prices.
4. Try different bundles.
5. Try different audiences.
6. Once a winner is found, **scale it**.

7. If the results are not what you need, move on to the next product.
Patience with one product: a store takes months to form its brand.

Keep a product in testing **until its data confirms it works**.
Only then add more products to the store.
A failed brand can be tested again once you have improved offers, upsells (extra offers after the first purchase) and creatives.

Apply what you learned from the first attempt before retrying.
Do not use it as a reason to abandon the brand category (the whole type of product).
Test pace and volume
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t:
Set a testing schedule of about **one or two products per week**.
Expect to test several products before finding a first winner.

Focus on controlling the inputs of testing, because results follow from consistent testing.
Test **one product per week** with a budget of about 200 to 300 USD per product.

Keep going until there is enough data to move on or keep trying.
Patience decides how many products you can test.
Choose a testing pace you can sustain.

Testing several products with high effort and all failing kills motivation.
Some operators can test **up to 15 products** when they have the energy.
That raises the chance that one of them becomes a winner.
Spam testing (testing many random products fast) only fits sellers who already know a very specific niche and have a large budget.

Without that knowledge and budget, it depends on luck and fails.
It needs funds for **50 to 60 products**.

Winning in dropshipping depends on continuous testing of many products and ads over time.
Each attempt has a low hit rate (chance of success).

More attempts raise the chance of finding a winner.
Stopping after a few failures makes a winner very unlikely.
Expect to test many products before finding a winner.

In the example, the first winner took about **three months** and about six tested products.
Test a product or strategy long enough before judging it.

A common budget is **about 30 products** before reassessing whether the approach works.
Most people quit after one or two tries, which is usually too early.

Do not wait for the one perfect winner before testing.
Keep testing many products until you see real progress.
A winner may not arrive on its own.

Taking action and testing many products matters more than finding the perfect first product.
Not every product will be a winner.

Keep testing rather than endlessly searching.
Find winners through **volume and speed of testing**, not through perfect products or perfect ads.

**Number of products before a first winner (sources differ; each reflects a different context):**
**Mentor's experience**

Number of products: Around the 8th product, range 5th to 20th
Context: Beginners
**Experienced sellers**

Number of products: About 5 products; TikTok process about 7 to 8 product tests
Context: Experienced sellers and TikTok
**Worked example**

Number of products: About 6 products over about 3 months
Context: Single example
**Minimum before judging**
Test pace and volume (continued)
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t:
Number of products: At least 12 products
Context: Before judging whether the approach works
**Test-count target**

Number of products: 20 to 30 products
Context: Before deciding a product is not a winner
**Reassessment budget**

Number of products: About 30 products
Context: Before reassessing the approach
**Operator example**

Number of products: 65 products over about 8 months
Context: One winner, scaled to roughly 200k USD revenue
**Spam testing**

Number of products: 50 to 60 products
Context: Only with specific niche knowledge and large budget
**Before first winner (one case)**

Number of products: More than 12 products
Context: Case with $1,000 daily revenue on day two
Plan for **many failed products** before a winner appears.

Expecting the first winner within the first three or four products is unrealistic, although it is not impossible.
Plan for the first product, and often the second, to **fail**.

Neither is likely to be a winner.
Expect several test rounds before finding a product that sells profitably.

Most beginners do not find a first winning product on the first try.
Keep testing products consistently and stay patient.

Taking a first product all the way to the scaling stage is already a **strong result** for a beginner.
Many people never get that far.

A second product can still fail, so one failed launch does not mean the method is wrong.
Apply what the earlier product taught you to the next launch.
Study the complete method (the full set of steps) and **test at least 12 products** before judging whether the approach works.

Testing 12 products is the point where beginners typically start to see results.
Most beginners who fail quit before reaching it.
Judging a new product after only one week and one sale is too early (see the kill rules section).

A beginner with no website or online advertising experience can learn both from freely available online guidance.
Then improve through repeated tests.

Expect early ad spend without returns during this phase.
Track results from the first campaign (one set of ads run together) so that losses stay within a set limit.
Note: this advice is from 2021 to 2022 and is older.
Patience with data
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t:
Be **patient** when a product is higher ticket (more expensive).
Give ads **more spend** (money put into ads) before closing them.
Keep them running while CTR (click-through rate, the share of viewers who click) is **above 1.5%**.

The start is the **hardest phase**, because every test costs money before a winner is found.
Once a product is making money, spending on testing becomes **much easier**.
Losing money on ads is a common reason people **quit** e-commerce (selling products online).

Organic work (free posting and visibility, not paid ads) mainly costs **time**, not cash.
Starting with organic **reduces the risk** of spending a large budget without results.

Viewing a product test as **time spent**, not money lost, is a valid way to keep testing without pressure.
Frustration after each failed product is common.

**Forcing results** quickly tends to make testing harder.
Judge a product using the **test window** (the set period of testing) and the data, not the first few clicks.
Influencer (a person with an audience who promotes products) results are not visible **immediately**.

Qualify influencers over a **longer period**, using the full funnel (the whole path from seeing an ad to buying).
Be **patient** while a product's data builds up.
Early-traffic randomness (results that swing by chance in the first visitors) means major changes should wait about **three weeks**.
In a slow period, take a **short break** to rest and plan ahead.
Then use the time to **tighten spending** on low-converting keywords (search words that show your ads but rarely lead to a sale), instead of cutting all paid traffic (visitors who come from ads).

Tightening is more effective than a **full stop**.
Note: this advice is from 2021 to 2022 and is **older**.

A product's kill rule (a fixed rule for when to stop a product) may need more data before it can be judged.
A **fixed test spend** still decides.

Build a sustainable pace with **patience**: "Patience decides how many products you can test."
Be **patient** with the number of products tested.

Do not expect results from **one trial**.
Keep **spare capital** (money kept aside and not used for tests), so that a slow product does not force an early decision.
Ad-level patience: a Facebook ad set (a group of ads that share an audience and budget) may need **more spend** before it shows whether it converts (leads to a sale).
Hook patience: a hook (the first seconds of an ad that grab attention) should be judged after **three to six repeated uploads** (putting the same ad live again).
Data over emotion
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t: Emotional attachment to products can cloud **optimisation decisions** (changes made to improve results).
Do not decide to **bid higher** (pay more per click) because you hope a product will improve.
Base all pausing and bidding decisions on **statistical thresholds** (fixed number cut-offs that data must reach) and historical data.

Do not base decisions on **optimism** about future performance.
Do not become emotionally attached to a product.

**Decide to kill or keep** it based on test data.
Failed stores and products should be **cut quickly** to free budget for new tests.

Treat ad testing as a **data-driven game**.
Decide based on CTR, store conversion rate (the share of store visitors who buy) and profit.

Do not fall in love with a product after investing time and money into it.
Do not become emotionally tied to a product you have **invested heavily** in.

The effort put in does not **guarantee** output, so judge it by the numbers.
Do not let emotional attachment **drive decisions**.
A product that looks good to you may **fail the numbers**, and a product that looks weak may sell.

Use the numbers on the screen as the **only signal** of whether something works.
This includes changes to ads, pages and budgets.
Compare each product test with **earlier data**, rather than with how the idea feels.
Letting go of products
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t: **Pick products** you actually enjoy testing.

Products you dislike are often dropped after **four days to a week and a half** of daily uploads.
Lack of motivation kills tests **before they produce data**.

Set a **kill rule** before you test, and follow it.
**Do not get attached** to one dropshipping product (selling products that a supplier ships to buyers, with no stock kept).
A failing product blocks budget that another product could use.
After a failed product, the **fastest comeback** is to reuse a proven creative (an ad image or video that already worked) and page template (a ready page layout).

**Switch** to a product that is already selling in the market.
Do not build fresh creatives from scratch.

When a product works at first and then stops being profitable at scale (spending more on what works), **drop it**.
Then launch the next product.

Keep the **next product** in the testing queue.
A product that flops should be replaced by the next product in the queue.
It should **not** be treated as proof that the business model (how the whole business earns money) does not work.

A product with a strong **visual wow factor** (a striking look that impresses at first) can still lack a clear problem it solves.
Such products often get **views without sales**.
Keep the kill rule even when the product looks impressive.
**Lean on the kill rule** when the product is one you like: "Set kill rules for a product before you test it and follow them, because keeping a product you like without results wastes time."

Do not stay with an idea just because it sounded good.
Test it and let the **result decide**.
Expecting failure
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t: Expect many ideas to **fail**.
Some tests will not work, and a few may cause problems such as **banned ad accounts** (accounts shut off by the ad platform).

Treat failed tests as part of the process and **keep testing**.
**Enjoy the process** of testing.

Brand (the name and look of your store), entry point (the first product or offer a buyer sees) and offer tests take time.
Many of them will **fail before one works**.

Expect many conversion tests to fail.
Treat each failure as a **learning step**.

Plan tests so that you know what is being tested and what the results are, then change the approach for the next test.
Note: this advice is from 2021 to 2022 and is **older**.
Most products fail in testing, and **no formula** reliably finds a winner on the first try.

Test many products, learn from each failure, and improve the process rather than expecting a **shortcut**.
Expect many test products to **fail**.

Repeated **iteration** (repeating and improving a test) is part of the process.
A failed launch is **not a verdict** on the whole business.
There is **no shortcut formula** that guarantees a winning product on the first try.
Winners come from testing many products, learning from losses, improving the process and the branding, and accepting that a few products will fail.

The first and often the second product are likely to fail, so plan for **several test rounds**.
Losses are a **normal part** of testing.

Before seeing any profit, a beginner should expect to lose about **$2,000 or the full budget**, as noted above.
Testing a product is a risk: a product can **fail quickly**.

So keep **spare capital**.
Intuition (gut feeling) often misjudges the market, so expect to be **wrong often**.
Plan for failure as the **default**.
Treat each failed product as **information**.

**Failure is feedback**, not the end: "A failed test is feedback, not failure. Test, refine and improve until the product or approach wins."
Many ideas fail.
Expecting failure (continued)
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t:
**Keep testing**, measure the results and adjust quickly.
Ad-level failure is **common**: "Some tests will not work, and a few may cause problems such as banned ad accounts."

Influencer campaigns **often fail**.
Some of the first creators (people who make content for social media) contacted will not convert.

The start is the **hardest phase**, because every test costs money before a winner is found.
Failure in one area does **not mean the model fails**.
Apply what each failure teaches to the **next product**.
The formula for lasting success in dropshipping is the **repetition of three elements**: a good product, strong creatives and a good funnel.

Repeat these elements **over time**.
Without this cycle, sustainable profitability (profit that lasts over time) cannot be achieved.

Build a consistent **pipeline** (a steady queue of ready items) of products and angles (different selling messages).
A single result does **not prove** a product will last.

**Create a routine**: test, read metrics (the numbers that show results), improve, and record.
Over time the routine builds the skills to recognise winners **faster**.

**Record** what was learned from each product so the next launch is better.
Write down the expected testing loss before starting.

Keep the **testing budget** (money set aside only for tests) separate from the core business.
Treat each product as a **single cycle** in a repeatable system.

Judge it by its data, record the result and **move to the next product** if the data says so.
Winning in dropshipping comes from **volume and speed** of testing.

A stalled result (one that stops moving) shows what does not work and brings you closer to what does.
Use a **fixed testing budget** and fixed kill rules as the system.

This way each product gets the same treatment.
Test many products in a **steady rhythm**.
Do not wait for the one perfect winner.

Store and brand building happen **after** the product is proven, not before.
**Constant testing** creates a stream of creatives and products to choose from.

Use a **cut rule** (a rule for when to stop) before the test starts, and follow it strictly.
The cycle of testing, measuring and adjusting **repeats** for each product.
**Keep testing** new products and angles to build a consistent pipeline.
Scaling, automation and channel notes
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t: **Procedure** for paid traffic automation work (software doing ad work for paid visitors):
1. Test **automated bidding** (software that picks how much to pay per click) with a controlled experiment (a test where only one thing changes).
2. Improve the **product feed** (the product list sent to ad platforms) to get more traffic.
3. Use **Smart Shopping** (an automated Google shopping ad type) in controlled tests, not on the whole account at once.
4. Shift the time saved to **higher-leverage activities** (tasks that gain the most).
Automating everything at once and checking performance only **once a month** lets underperformance run for weeks unnoticed.

Introduce automation **in steps** with regular review.
Blind trust in automated results is the **most common error**.

Automation works like an exoskeleton (a wearable frame that helps a person lift more).
It lets the marketer handle **much more volume** without more strain.

It does **not replace judgement**.
Use it to get more done with the **same effort**.

The basics of paid advertising stay the same whatever the interface (the screen or tool you use).
Show the **right message** to the right person at the right time.
If a campaign ignores this, for example by targeting (choosing who sees the ads) an audience that has no reason to buy, it will **underperform**.

This happens regardless of tool changes.
Scaling speed **differed** among operators (the people who run the business).
One reached **25k plus per month** within two months from start.
Another needed **six months** before mentorship (guidance from an experienced coach) and three months after.
One scaled **within three days** once a winning product and offer were found.
Scaling, automation and channel notes (continued)
p.s: Run tests with budgets, hypotheses and kill rules

p.t: The **bottleneck** (the one step that slows everything) was finding a working offer, not the scaling itself.

Build the mindset of **right traffic, right time and right price** before setting up any campaigns.
The later campaign work depends on these concepts.
Checking targeting against the funnel stage (where a visitor is in the buying path) and the **cost of acquisition** (cost to win one buyer) is the core test for every paid campaign.

Paid ad management should be based on **profitability** (making more than you spend), rather than raw traffic volume.
Note: this advice is from 2021 to 2022 and is **older**.
Ad testing decisions are made on CTR, store conversion rate and profit.
**Ad-account quality** (the health of your advertising account): the bigger the account, the more the testing loss can grow.

A winning product found in one test may need an **offer change** (a new deal or price) before it scales.
**Test before scaling**.

Do not scale a product that has not shown data.
A single operator scaled one winner to roughly **200k USD** in revenue after **65 products**.
Afterwards the brand, run as a **custom brand** (a brand with its own name and look), was still growing day over day and month over month.
Test new and unconventional ideas if the **risk is low** and the potential loss is small.

**Assess the downside** (what could go wrong) before rejecting ideas.
Then measure their impact on the brand.
A fall sock product was a **one-size-fits-all** product (one size fits everyone) with three pack sizes.

Its broad audience was moms, teens and **Q4 gift buyers** (shoppers buying from October to December).
The store was put up in about **15 minutes**.

The lifestyle and emotional ads were mixed and matched to fit the fall look.
The seller's conversion rate was **strong**.

The product was scaled for a period **before the season ended**.
It **would not sell in summer** and would fade as a trend.
